A taxon is Critically Endangered when the best available evidence indicates that it meets any of the criteria for Critically Endangered and it is therefore considered to be facing an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild.
Critically endangered, possibly extinct

A taxon is Data Deficient when there is inadequate information to make a direct or indirect assessment of its risk of extinction based on its distribution and/or population status. A taxon in this category may have been studied in depth and its biology may be well known, but appropriate data on abundance and/or distribution are lacking. Data Deficient is therefore not a Threatened category. Listing a taxon in this category indicates that more information is required and does not rule out the possibility that future research will show that the taxon could have been classified in a Threatened category. It is imperative to make full use of all available data.

A taxon is Endangered when the best available evidence indicates that it meets any of the criteria for Endangered and it is therefore considered to be facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild.

A taxon is Extinct in the Wild when it is known only to survive in cultivation, in captivity or as a naturalised population (or populations) well outside its past range. A taxon is presumed Extinct in the Wild when detailed surveys in known and/or expected habitat, at appropriate times (diurnal, seasonal, annual), throughout its historic range have failed to record a single individual. Surveys should be over a time frame appropriate to the taxon's life cycle and life form.

A taxon is Extinct when there is no doubt that the last individual has died. A taxon is presumed Extinct when exhaustive surveys in its known and/or expected habitat, at appropriate times (diurnal, seasonal, annual), throughout its historic range have failed to record a single individual. Surveys should be over a time frame appropriate to the taxon's life cycle and life form.

A taxon is Least Concern when it has been evaluated against the criteria and does not qualify for Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable or Near Threatened. Widespread and abundant taxa are included in this category.

Category reserved for a taxon considered ineligible for assessment at the regional level. A taxon may be classed NA because it is not a wild population or is not within its natural range in the region, or because it is a vagrant in the region. A taxon may also be classed NA because it occurs only in very low numbers in the region (e.g. when the regional Red List authority has decided to use a 'filter' to exclude some taxa before the assessment procedure) or because it is classified at a lower taxonomic level (e.g. below the species or subspecies level) than those considered eligible by the regional Red List authority. Unlike other Red List categories, it is not mandatory to assign the NA category to all taxa to which it applies, but it is recommended where it is informative.
A taxon is Not Evaluated when it has not yet been evaluated against the criteria.

A taxon is Near Threatened when it has been evaluated against the criteria and does not, for the time being, qualify for Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable, but is close to qualifying for a Threatened category or is likely to qualify in the near future.

Category assigned to a taxon when there is no reasonable doubt that the last individual capable of reproduction in the region has died or has disappeared from the wild in the region, or, in the case of a former visiting taxon, when the last individual has died or disappeared from the wild in the region. The time limit chosen for listing a taxon as RE is left to the discretion of the regional Red List authority, but should not normally be earlier than the year 1500 CE.
A taxon is Vulnerable when the best available evidence indicates that it meets any of the criteria for Vulnerable and it is therefore considered to be facing a high risk of extinction in the wild.

Purely 'observational' or 'correlative' experimentation and research must be placed in the 'inventories' or 'monitoring/surveillance' categories.
Data acquisition is carried out with a specific approach involving several of the approaches described above.

Occurrence data acquisition is carried out with the aim of obtaining information on the presence/absence or numbers/abundance (count…) of one or more biodiversity objects. The collection scheme is designed to provide a spatial representation of the distribution of one or more biodiversity objects at predefined dates or periods.

Occurrence data acquisition is carried out with a collection scheme involving repeated acquisition over time. The approach allows a state to be compared between different periods for one or more biodiversity objects. It is set up in connection with a predetermined theme (conservation biology, global change, …).

Participatory observation programmes (general public or volunteer experts, 'recording scheme'), collecting observation data without any particular sampling design or predefined objective. Field notebook entry falls under this heading. Likewise, incidental observations (non-target group) made during a specific programme fall into this category. If this information is collected in an online atlas programme, it falls into category 1.2

Project-based approach with sampling aimed at covering as much territory as possible for a given species or taxonomic group, in order to establish its distribution in an atlas approach, whatever its scale (generally departmental, regional or national). When the distribution inventory is the dominant approach and is accompanied by occasional observations (non-target: e.g. observation of a grass snake during a breeding bird atlas square), these occasional observations may be included in this category but should as far as possible form a separate dataset within the same acquisition framework with the category 'opportunistic naturalist observations'

label_en: Inventory for species or community study
definition_en: Data acquisition approach associated with a protocol aimed at obtaining information on the factors that structure the presence and/or observation of a species, population or community at the scale of a station or an eco-complex. Objectives may be multiple (conservation, ethology, population dynamics, biological interactions, community structuring ...). Setting up protocols to establish detectability indices for species and/or their degree of specialisation with respect to a habitat falls into this case.

Dataset generated by mobilising (entering) data from one or more specimen collections (herbarium, entomological collection etc.) with the aim of making them available for any use. This case is to be used only if no other more specific reason underlying the constitution of the collection can be assigned: for example, where an exploration campaign generates collections, the dataset must be assigned to the 'ATBI and exploration' objective (cf. label 2.5)

Special case of a dataset containing only data derived from the analysis of literature (whether published or grey literature) with the aim of making them available for any use. This case is to be used only if no other more specific reason underlying the constitution of the literature can be assigned: for example, where an exploration campaign on a site generates publications, the dataset must be assigned to the 'ATBI and exploration' objective. Field observation notebooks rather fall under 1.1, Opportunistic observations

Data corresponding to vegetation-habitat-ecosystem mapping established at a broad scale (department, region, PNR, small natural region) and not according to a site or site-network approach. Field approaches, image processing or a combination of both are included. Species community relevés (generally vegetation/phytosociological relevés or benthos for marine habitats) carried out as part of vegetation-habitat-ecosystem mapping. If only relevés are carried out (without determination of the vegetation or habitat type), another heading must be assigned.

Spatial sampling design with determination of the vegetation-habitat-ecosystem type. Species community relevés (generally vegetation/phytosociological relevés or benthos for marine habitats) carried out as part of a vegetation-habitat-ecosystem inventory. If only relevés are carried out (without determination of the vegetation or habitat type), another heading must be assigned
Record of the presence of a vegetation-habitat-ecosystem type not falling within a predefined sampling design

Species community relevés (generally vegetation/phytosociological relevés or benthos for marine habitats) carried out for studies or research on vegetation-habitats-ecosystems. Data acquisition approach associated with a protocol aimed at improving knowledge or the definition of a habitat, building a typology, or clarifying its functioning, assessing its conservation status... If only relevés are carried out (unrelated to the vegetation or habitat type), another heading must be assigned (1.3)

Special case of a dataset containing only data derived from the analysis of literature (whether published or grey literature) with the aim of making them available for any use concerning habitats and the associated standardised relevés (phytosociological, benthos)

Inventories carried out as part of producing a municipal biodiversity atlas, whether following the 'Ministry' approach or a similar approach (PNR approach, IBC for example). Pre-existing data digitised on the occasion of and for the ABC fall into this category. Any temporal monitoring initiated in an ABC does not fall under this heading

Acquisition of field data (not synthesis) to establish/confirm or update ZNIEFF inventory zones (and possible ZICO or IBA type approaches). Inventories to support the management of (already designated) areas fall under the next heading (3.3)

Structured acquisition of naturalist data to prepare, revise or update a management plan (in the broad sense) of a natural area with a particular protection or management status (Natura 2000, Reserves, Parks, public forest...) or of a private site for its ecological management (e.g. golf courses, LGV right-of-way...). Including assessments to evaluate the heritage value of the site (IQE type), the conservation status of its habitats, to define issues by sector... 'Opportunistic' data collected by these managers may also fall into this category but should preferably form datasets separate from protocol-based data (cat. 2.4)

Opportunistic data collected in a site-centred approach: during management operations, related observation data collected during a site inventory or monitoring. The notion of site covers a predefined area (or network of areas) with a management issue (reserves, conservancy site, company sites, green space...)

Programme targeted at one or a few sites, aimed at compiling an extensive inventory of the taxa present, multi-group and generally to discover new species (for Science or for the territory). Examples: ATBI, IBG... These programmes generally include collection building, barcoding, taxonomic work etc. Inventory work on a site covering a very large invertebrate order (Hymenoptera, or Diptera, Coleoptera or Lepidoptera, Arachnida etc.) falls into this category

Inventories carried out as part of regulatory impact assessment or incidence assessment procedures, before the impacts occur. Post-construction regulatory monitoring (e.g. bat mortality) or compensation monitoring is not covered by this category (falls under category 5.4)

Data corresponding to vegetation-habitat-ecosystem mapping for a site, to support management (identification of issues, adaptation of management etc.) Field approaches, image processing or a combination of both are included. Species community relevés (generally vegetation/phytosociological relevés or benthos for marine habitats) carried out as part of an inventory or mapping of the vegetation-habitats-ecosystems of a site. If only relevés are carried out (without determination of the vegetation or habitat type), another heading must be assigned.
Fish, fisheries, halieutic, game, pharmaceutical or dendrological inventories and monitoring to quantify the available resource, stocks or harvests taken (game bag...)
Census and monitoring of wildlife / linear transport infrastructure collision points. Monitoring of marine animal strandings (turtles, cetaceans...) is also placed under this heading
Work, generally in the research field, aimed at studying behaviour at the individual level: dispersal, movement path, migratory path, space use at different periods... etc.

This category only includes data obtained according to a protocol repeated over time which aims to provide a reliable picture of the evolution of the measured variables at the level of a population, a species or several species that do not however form an interacting community. It generally concerns a fairly large scale (site networks, departmental to national), generally representative, exhaustive or regular sampling, and does not directly aim to test a hypothesis with manipulation (if so, category 5.). Repeated atlases ultimately allowing changes in distribution to be measured fall into category 1.2

This category only includes data obtained according to a protocol of surveys of interacting species repeated over time, which aims to provide a reliable picture of the evolution over time of the measured variables for a species community, possibly linked to a habitat type. It concerns a fairly large scale (site networks, departmental to national), generally representative, exhaustive or regular sampling, and does not directly aim to test a hypothesis with manipulation (if so, category 6.2 or 6.3)

This category only includes data obtained according to a protocol repeated over time which aims to provide a reliable picture of the evolution over time of the presence and/or area of a habitat in the broad sense (vegetation, ecosystem...). It generally concerns a fairly large scale (site networks, departmental to national), generally representative, exhaustive or regular sampling, and does not directly aim to test a hypothesis with manipulation (if so, category 6.2). Species community relevés (generally vegetation/phytosociological relevés or benthos for marine habitats) carried out for surveillance fall within this scope. If only relevés are carried out (without determination of the vegetation or habitat type), the previous heading must be assigned

label_en: Surveillance of pathogens and invasive alien species
definition_en: Schemes dedicated to detecting the presence (or abundance...) and monitoring the evolution of species having a negative impact on agriculture, forestry, health or biodiversity... Participatory or professional, surveys... Related observations from these protocols also fall into this category but should ideally form a separate dataset. Monitoring of so-called 'pest' species falls into this category

These are surveillance/watch schemes over time to detect, without prior assumptions, changes in the measured variables (abundance of a population of a species of concern, individual traits, abundance index, occupancy rate, traits and other species community metrics, area occupied by vegetation-habitats-ecosystems...). It concerns a local scale (site or predetermined network of sites – reserve networks etc.). Does not directly aim to test a hypothesis with manipulation (if so, category 6.2). Experimental design: time series

Monitoring over time (before/after, possibly with controls) linking species or communities, vegetation-habitats-ecosystems, and a management action (including non-intervention) or a pressure in order to determine its effect. Generally in a natural area context or for restoration or compensation (verification of a gain over time), or even research work. Generally concerns a site or a network of sites. Experimental design: B/A (before/after) and BACI (before/after control/impact) Any large-scale adaptive scheme would fall into this category

Study of the effects of management (or pressure, or non-management etc.) on species or communities, vegetation-habitats-ecosystems, with a space-for-time substitution. That is, the effect is measured only at a time t, by comparing different management histories but without before/after measurement (if before/after: 6.2). Experimental design: C/I (control/ impact)

These are temporal monitoring schemes aimed at tracking impacts after the installation of a structure, imposed by law or when works are authorised. For example, monitoring of bird and bat mortality after a wind farm is installed. Regulatory monitoring as part of compensation also falls into this category

Category to be used when the dataset mixes various types of data, without metadata currently allowing them to be separated into more precise and more coherent datasets. This may include acquisition frameworks and datasets made up of groupings of Elementary Exchange Data (DEE) to produce an atlas, only when the original data collection objective cannot be determined. When no information is available on the reasons for data acquisition, this heading must be used

Cases not clearly falling under the other headings. In this case the metadata (free 'description' and 'protocol' fields of the metadata records) must clearly explain the purpose of the data acquisition

A thallus is a vegetative body having neither leaves, nor stems, nor roots, produced by certain non-motile organisms.
A tuber is a storage organ, generally underground, ensuring the survival of plants during the winter season or in periods of drought, and often their vegetative propagation.
A bulb is a vertical underground shoot with modified leaves used as a food storage organ by a dormant plant.
The rhizome is an underground and sometimes subaquatic stem filled with food reserves in certain perennial plants.
The individual is at the emergent stage: emergence from the egg.
Stage immediately following the larval stage and showing certain juvenile characteristics.
Fruit: The individual is in the form of a fruit.
The individual has not yet reached the adult stage. It is a young individual.
Individual that has not reached sexual maturity.
Individual that has almost reached adult size but is not considered as such by its conspecifics.
Individual in the state in which it emerges from the egg, a state in which it spends a more or less long time before metamorphosis.
Eruciform larva of lepidopterans or butterflies.
Amphibian larva.

Unknown: the biological status of the individual is not known.
Not specified: the biological status of the individual has not been specified.
The individual is at the vegetative stage.
Undetermined: the biological status of the individual could not be determined.
Breeding: the observed subject is at the breeding stage (nesting, gravid, sporophore, flowering, fruiting…)
Hibernation: hibernation is a state of regulated hypothermia, lasting several days or weeks, that allows animals to conserve energy during winter.
Aestivation: aestivation is a phenomenon analogous to hibernation, during which animals fall into lethargy. Aestivation occurs during the hottest and driest periods of summer.
No breeding: indicates that the individual does not show breeding behaviour. In plants: absence of flowers, fruits…
Don't know: the information is not known

Not observed: the observer did not detect a particular taxon, searched for using the protocol appropriate to the location and date of the observation. The taxon may be present but not seen, temporarily absent, or truly absent.
Present: one or more individuals of the taxon were actually observed and/or signs indicating the presence of the taxon were found
Collection: the observation comes from a collection database.
Literature: the observation was extracted from a scientific article or book.
Don't know: the source is unknown.
Field: the observation comes directly from a database or document resulting from field survey.
Validation work has not yet been carried out. The validation status is pending

The record is accurate. There is no notable or significant doubt about the accuracy of the observation or of the taxon identification. Validation was carried out in particular on the basis of evidence of the observation confirming the producer's identification, or after checking with the observer and/or the identifier.

The record has a good level of reliability. It is plausible and credible. There is, a priori, no reason to doubt the accuracy of the record, but insufficient additional elements are available or assessed (in particular evidence or the possibility of returning to the source record) to assign a higher level of certainty.
The record is unlikely or surprising, but there are insufficient elements to establish an obvious error. The record is considered doubtful.

The record has been refuted (obvious/proven error) or has too low a level of reliability. It is considered too improbable (aberrant in particular with regard to the known range, the biotic and abiotic parameters of the taxon's ecological niche, or the evidence reveals an identification error). It is considered invalid.

The record went through the whole validation process, but the operator (human or machine) could not decide on the level of reliability, in particular for the following reasons: insufficient knowledge of the taxon, or insufficient information on the observation.
The validation status is not known.
Individual whose taxon has an unknown area of origin, so it cannot be said whether it is native or introduced.
Individual for which the information has not been provided.

Individual of a taxon present in the broad sense in the geographic area considered, i.e. a native taxon or a taxon for which it is not known whether it belongs to one of the other categories. Lack of knowledge therefore favours native status.  Native means: a taxon that originates from the geographic area considered and has developed there naturally without human contribution, or a taxon that arrived there without human intervention (intentional or not) from an area in which it is native6.  (NB: excludes hybrids at least one of whose parents is introduced in the area considered)  All taxa categorised as 'native' or 'indigenous' are grouped under this status.  Taxa wintering for a few months of the year fall into this category.

Taxon introduced (established or possibly established) at the local level.  Introduced means: a taxon whose local presence is due to human intervention, intentional or not, or a taxon that arrived in the area without human intervention but from an area in which it is introduced.  Established (term used for fauna, naturalised for flora) means: an introduced taxon that forms viable (reproducing) and lasting populations that persist in the wild without the need for human intervention.  This status groups all taxa categorised as « non-indigenous », « exotic », « exogenous », « allogenic », « allochthonous », « non-native », « naturalised » in a scientific publication.

Individual of a locally introduced taxon that produces fertile offspring, often in large numbers, and has the potential to spread exponentially over a large area, thus rapidly increasing its range. This often leads to negative ecological, economic or health consequences. This status groups all individuals of taxa categorised as "introduced invasive", "exotic invasive", or "invasive".
Individual whose taxon is introduced, which occasionally reproduces outside its area of cultivation or captivity, but cannot persist in the wild.
Individual whose taxon is occasional, non-breeding, accidental or exceptional in the geographical area considered (for example a passage migrant), which is local.
Don't know: the collection technique used is not known
In situ: direct observation in the field (walked through or along). Corresponds to Direct daytime terrestrial observation in the CAMPANULE database
